Astrophysical plasmas are known to be magnetized and turbulent
Magnetization of these fluids most frequently arises from the dynamo action to which turbulence is an essential component
Turbulence in weakly magnetized conducting fluid converts about 10% of the energy of the cascade into the magnetic field
Magnetic fields will come to equipartition with turbulent motions in about 10 eddy turnover times
The Reynolds numbers are typically very large in astrophysical flows as the scales are large
For instance, Re numbers of 10^10 are very common for astrophysical flows
The drivers of turbulence, e.g. supernovae explosions in the interstellar medium, inject energy at large scales and then the energy cascades down to small scales through a hierarchy of eddies
The famous Kolmogorov picture corresponds to hydrodynamic turbulence, but a qualitatively similar turbulence also develops in magnetized fluids/plasmas
Simulations of interstellar medium, accretion disks and other astrophysical environments also produce turbulent picture, provided that the simulations are not dominated by numerical viscosity
The definitive confirmation of turbulence presence comes from observations, e.g. observations of electron density fluctuations in the interstellar medium
The spectral index of the Big Power Law in the Sky coincides with the Kolmogorov one
The GS95 theory assumes the isotropic injection of energy at scale L and the injection velocity equal to the Alfvén velocity in the fluid V
The Alfvén Mach number A = V/L is the ratio of the eddy turnover rate t_1 = V/L and the viscous dissipation rate t_1 = h/L^2
The weak turbulence is wave-like turbulence with wave packets undergoing many collisions before transferring energy to small scales
The strong turbulence is eddy-like with cascading happening similar to Kolmogorov turbulence within roughly an eddy turnover time
The LV99 model generalizes the Sweet-Parker one by accounting for the existence of magnetic field line stochasticity and turbulent field wandering
Magnetic field wandering is a characteristic feature of magnetized turbulence in 3D
The Sweet-Parker model considers magnetic fields that are laminar and therefore the frozen-in condition is violated only over a thin layer dominated by plasma resistivity
The LV99 model accounts for the existence of magnetic field line stochasticity and turbulent field wandering
Eddy advection of heat dominates in many astrophysically-motivated cases
Thermal conductivity arises from electrons streaming along stochastic magnetic field lines
Subdiffusion is a process where the diffusion coefficient decreases with time and requires rather restrictive settings
Superdiffusion is a process where the diffusion coefficient increases with time and is possible on scales smaller than the injection scale of turbulence
